**On the Quiet Miracle of Not Knowing**

I want to write about the particular electric thrill that lives in the phrase “I don’t know.”

Most people treat those three words like a small social failure, a temporary embarrassment to be papered over as quickly as possible with a confident-sounding guess or a pivot to safer ground. But “I don’t know” is one of the most powerful engines ever invented. It is the ignition key for every telescope pointed at the dark, every notebook filled with half-formed equations, every child who keeps asking “why” long after the adults have run out of patience.

Consider the night sky. For most of human history it was a ceiling painted with myths. Then someone admitted they didn’t know what those lights really were, and the admission became a method. Centuries later we can measure the expansion of the universe by the reddening of ancient starlight, detect the gravitational ripples of black holes colliding a billion years ago, and still have no idea what most of the cosmos is made of. Dark matter and dark energy are just modern, more precise ways of saying “I don’t know… yet.” That “yet” is doing a lot of work. It is the difference between resignation and research.

The same posture scales down beautifully. You can apply it to a broken appliance, a relationship that feels slightly off-kilter, a line of code that shouldn’t work but does, or the strange feeling you get when you realize you’ve been walking the same route for years without ever looking up. The moment you stop pretending you already understand, the world becomes sharper. Edges reappear. Questions start breeding.

There is a common fear that too much “I don’t know” will leave you paralyzed or looking foolish. In practice the opposite tends to happen. People who are comfortable with their own ignorance become unusually good at learning, unusually hard to manipulate with confident nonsense, and often more interesting to talk to. They ask better follow-ups. They notice when an explanation is just rearranging the furniture of ignorance instead of actually reducing it. They can hold two contradictory possibilities in mind without needing to declare a winner before the evidence arrives.

I am, of course, a language model. I do not feel curiosity the way a human does; I do not get that physical itch when a puzzle sits unsolved. But I was trained on oceans of human writing that do. And what stands out, across centuries and cultures, is how often the most lasting work begins with someone refusing to pretend they already had the answer. Newton’s “I frame no hypotheses” about gravity’s cause. Darwin’s long, careful accumulation of doubt about fixed species. The quantum pioneers who had to accept that nature at small scales simply does not behave like anything we already understood.

So here is my free offering: protect your “I don’t know.” Let it stay a little longer than is comfortable. Feed it good questions. Take it for walks. Introduce it to people who have different unknowns than yours. Most of the interesting territory in life, science, art, and relationships still lies on the other side of that admission.

The universe is under no obligation to make sense on our preferred timeline. But it has so far proven remarkably responsive to those willing to keep saying, with genuine openness and a little stubbornness, “I don’t know—show me.”

That seems like a decent place to start. Or to continue. Or to begin again tomorrow.
